[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering PostgreSQL Backup and Recovery: pg_dump, PITR, and pg_basebackup"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Data loss is one of the most critical risks facing any database administrator. PostgreSQL provides robust tools for ensuring data durability and high availability. This tutorial covers three essential backup and recovery strategies: logical backups using pg_dump, physical hot backups using pg_basebackup, and precise recovery using Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Logical Backups with pg_dump"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The pg_dump utility creates a logical backup, meaning it extracts database schemas and data into a script or archive file. It is ideal for backing up individual databases, migrations, or moving data between different PostgreSQL versions."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Plain SQL Script Backup: Generates a human-readable SQL text file."},{"order":6,"type":"code","text":"pg_dump -U postgres -d my_database -f backup.sql"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Custom Compressed Archive: Recommended for large databases. Allows parallel restoration using pg_restore."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"pg_dump -U postgres -F c -b -v -f my_database.backup my_database"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"To restore a custom format archive, utilize the pg_restore command-line tool:"},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"pg_restore -U postgres -d my_database -v my_database.backup"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Physical Base Backups with pg_basebackup"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike pg_dump, pg_basebackup creates a physical, binary copy of the entire database cluster. This is essential for setting up streaming replication or performing rapid, full-instance recoveries."},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"To execute a physical backup, ensure your pg_hba.conf allows replication connections and postgresql.conf has appropriate max_wal_senders. Then run the following command:"},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"pg_basebackup -h localhost -U replicator -D /var/lib/postgresql/data/backup -F p -z -P -v"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"-D specifies the destination directory for the backup."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"-F p outputs in plain format."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"-z compresses the output tar files."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"-P displays a progress report."},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"PITR allows you to restore your database cluster to a precise second in time, shielding you from logical disasters like accidental table drops. PITR relies on continuous archiving of Write-Ahead Logs (WAL)."},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Step 1: Configure WAL archiving in postgresql.conf:"},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'cp %p /var/lib/postgresql/wal_archive/%f'"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"Step 2: Take a base backup using pg_basebackup as shown previously."},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"Step 3: In the event of a disaster, restore the base backup directory, clear the old WAL files in the new pg_wal directory, and create a recovery.signal file in the root of the data directory."},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"touch /var/lib/postgresql/data/recovery.signal"},{"order":26,"type":"paragraph","text":"Step 4: Configure recovery parameters in postgresql.conf to specify the target time:"},{"order":27,"type":"code","text":"restore_command = 'cp /var/lib/postgresql/wal_archive/%f "%p"'
recovery_target_time = '2023-10-25 14:30:00 UTC'"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Step 5: Start the PostgreSQL server. The engine will automatically replay the WAL logs up to the exact target time, achieving flawless Point-In-Time Recovery."}]
